0.text: Not sure if it would necessarily fit here in the bulleted section, due to length, but since you mentioned Irenaeus of Lyon: in Against Heresies, Book II, Chapter 34, where he affirms annihilationism, he both discusses Luke 16:19-31 and, later in the chapter, makes that same point about God sustaining those for as long as He wills (and how He will nto sustain he wicked forever).

4.author: Joseph Dear
4.text: Just to ensure internal consistency, what do you mean by "spiritually immortal"? Earlier you had mentioned spiritual death as the soul dying like the body. Is "spiritual immortality" meant as the soul living on? If so, is that only for the saved?

5.author: Phil Welch
5.text: Specifically I was commenting on how (per 1 Peter 1:23) when we are born again, we are born of imperishable seed (and yet our bodies are still, until the second coming, perishable), so this seems to be a spiritual thing that happens at conversion.  Since we will not undergo the 'second death', our soul will live on forever, unlike the unsaved.

6.author: Phil Welch
6.text: I hadn't been putting scripture references in the short version since the full arguments were in their respective sections below, but I can see the value of including them up here unless you think it makes it less readable / more clunky.

7.author: Joseph Dear
7.text:
This is theological/philosophical advantage to annihilationism that has hit me recently. We can focus more on the good news of eternal life with Jesus, rather than what you escape. In fact, while annihilation is terrifying, it is terrifying because of what you lose, so even then it is all about the good things to be gained.
When eternal conscious hell in fiery torture is the alternative, you necessarily will have to give some focus to that. Even spending eternity in a stuffy room made of concrete that smells and has no bedding to sleep on it immeasurably better than hell and is worth any earthly sacrifice. The goodness of what we gain becomes an afterthought.

8.author: Phil Welch
8.text: It has changed the way I evangelize.  I do door-to-door (I'm a non-denom. evangelical) and several people in the group I go with will use hell to 'up the stakes' when conversing with people, and I now find myself trying to realign the conversations to the gift of eternal life.

9.author: Joseph Dear
9.text: This would be the one place I would disagree, since I believe even the devil and co. will be destroyed. That would go into more depth than a Google Doc comment can provide, of course, but if you are interested in why I believe that, we can always discuss it further.

10.author: Phil Welch
10.text: I added a link in the full #30 section to your section on Rev. 20:10, but had been hesitant to put a full discussion on it because this is the one area where I feel it has less immediate/practical implications for our life now and so is less important to me than the main topic.  And I am worried that if people don't go deep enough to find out whether not taking Rev 20:10 literally is correct, they may have a more immediate reaction like "you're ignoring the literal meanings of the words" which may cause them to pull away from the whole conversation.

11.author: Joseph Dear
11.text: It seems clear on its face that the claim that Jesu spoke more about hell than heaven is false because almost every mention of hell also mentions heaven, yet there are independent mentions of heaven too. But have you assembled a list, to come up with the 3x figure. i would be interested in hearing more about this, since this hell more than heaven thing is such a cliche.

16.author: Joseph Dear
16.text:
While Aquinas of course did believe in eternal torment, from what I can tell he was actually rebutting this view here, not endorsing it. As he did at various points in Summa Theologica, he posits views and then rebuts them. Ths is Summa Theologica, Ia2ae. 87, 4, right (translations differ a lot)?
https://www.newadvent.org/summa/2087.htm

21.author: Joseph Dear
21.text:
This view also makes the whole idea of eternal torment in its prooftexts kinda silly. Do people go to "eternal punishment", or "finite punishment that would end if you stopped isnning but you won't."
It also renders the finite sin argument pointless.
And why put people in "eternal fire" if the punishment isn't itself meant to be eternal, but only is because it keeps getting extended?

23.author: Joseph Dear
23.text: Do you believe the destruction fo Edom is future? Because if it was about the then-future but now-past destruction of the ancient kingdom of Edom, then the smoke rising forever isn't even literal (since Edom isn't still burning)?

24.author: Phil Welch
24.text: Great point - I believe it was a past event and that the smoke rising forever wasn't literal as stated - added!

25.author: Joseph Dear
25.text: On what basis do you come up with the interpretation that the beast and false prophet are spiritual beings like the devil - especially given the angel's explanation of the beast in 17:9-14.

26.author: Phil Welch
26.text: On the basis of my very difficult time interpreting Revelation!  I have been favoring the idea of the Beast being a spiritual entity comprised of separate physical entities (actual unbelieving humans/rulers) and that the individual physical entities will not suffer eternal torment, but the spiritual entity will.  Totally weak in this area and open to correction/clarification.

27.author: Joseph Dear
27.text: There is also the utter inconsistency with how many traditionalists use John 17:3 to supposedly show that eternal life doesn't just mean literally living forever, but instead means a specific kind of life, i.e. knowing God. Which is it? Is eternal referring to quantity r is it symbolic of quality?
